claim: Replicability of previously-reported 'structural brain behavior' (SBB)-associations has been questioned recently.
source: Yet, replicability of the previously-reported 'structural brain behavior' (SBB)-associations has been questioned, recently.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study, referencing recent concerns in the field.

claim: Among healthy individuals, finding an association between performance at standard psychological tests and brain morphology is relatively unlikely.
source: Our results revealed that among healthy individuals 1) finding an association between performance at standard psychological tests and brain morphology is relatively unlikely
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's empirical investigation.

claim: Significant associations found using an exploratory approach have overestimated effect sizes.
source: Our results revealed that among healthy individuals 1) finding an association between performance at standard psychological tests and brain morphology is relatively unlikely 2) significant associations, found using an exploratory approach, have overestimated effect sizes
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's empirical investigation.

claim: Significant associations found using an exploratory approach can hardly be replicated in an independent sample.
source: Our results revealed that among healthy individuals 1) finding an association between performance at standard psychological tests and brain morphology is relatively unlikely 2) significant associations, found using an exploratory approach, have overestimated effect sizes and 3) can hardly be replicated in an independent sample.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's empirical investigation.

claim: Studies using in-vivo neuroimaging have provided compelling evidence of a relationship between human skills and traits and brain morphometry.
source: Studies using in-vivo neuroimaging have provided compelling evidence of a relationship between human skills and traits and brain morphometry that were further influenced by individuals' years of experience, as well as level of expertise.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the field.

claim: Brain morphometry is influenced by individuals' years of experience and level of expertise.
source: Studies using in-vivo neuroimaging have provided compelling evidence of a relationship between human skills and traits and brain morphometry that were further influenced by individuals' years of experience, as well as level of expertise.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the field.

claim: Subtle changes in brain structure were shown following new learning/training.
source: More subtle changes were also shown following new learning/training (Draganski et al., 2004; Taubert et al., 2011), hence further demonstrating dynamic relationships between behavioral performance and brain structural features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are dynamic relationships between behavioral performance and brain structural features.
source: More subtle changes were also shown following new learning/training (Draganski et al., 2004; Taubert et al., 2011), hence further demonstrating dynamic relationships between behavioral performance and brain structural features.
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies showing changes following learning/training.

claim: Studies have aimed to map inter-individual differences in personality traits to normal variations in brain morphology.
source: Such observations quickly generated a conceptual basis for growing number of studies aiming to map subtle inter-individual differences in observed behavior such as personality traits (Nostro et al., 2017), impulsivity traits (Matsuo et al., 2009) or political orientation (Kanai et al., 2011) to normal variations in brain morphology (for review see Genon et al., 2018; Kanai and Rees, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies have aimed to map inter-individual differences in impulsivity traits to normal variations in brain morphology.
source: Such observations quickly generated a conceptual basis for growing number of studies aiming to map subtle inter-individual differences in observed behavior such as personality traits (Nostro et al., 2017), impulsivity traits (Matsuo et al., 2009) or political orientation (Kanai et al., 2011) to normal variations in brain morphology (for review see Genon et al., 2018; Kanai and Rees, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies have aimed to map inter-individual differences in political orientation to normal variations in brain morphology.
source: Such observations quickly generated a conceptual basis for growing number of studies aiming to map subtle inter-individual differences in observed behavior such as personality traits (Nostro et al., 2017), impulsivity traits (Matsuo et al., 2009) or political orientation (Kanai et al., 2011) to normal variations in brain morphology (for review see Genon et al., 2018; Kanai and Rees, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The morphometry of the brain in humans is related to a wide spectrum of aspects observed in human behavior.
source: Altogether, these studies created an empirical background supporting the assumption that the morphometry of the brain in humans is related to the wide spectrum of aspects observed in human behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from previous studies.

claim: Reports on SBB associations may have important implications in psychological sciences and clinical research.
source: Such reports on structural brain behavior (SBB) associations may not only have important implications in psychological sciences and clinical research (Ismaylova et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2015; Luders et al., 2013; Luders et al., 2012; McEwen et al., 2016), but also possibly hold an important key for our understanding of brain functions (Genon et al., 2018) and thus concern many research fields including basic cognitive neuroscience.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SBB associations possibly hold an important key for our understanding of brain functions.
source: Such reports on structural brain behavior (SBB) associations may not only have important implications in psychological sciences and clinical research (Ismaylova et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2015; Luders et al., 2013; Luders et al., 2012; McEwen et al., 2016), but also possibly hold an important key for our understanding of brain functions (Genon et al., 2018) and thus concern many research fields including basic cognitive neuroscience.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a speculative statement about potential importance.

claim: Psychological sciences are affected by a general replication crisis.
source: Yet, along with the general replication crisis affecting psychological sciences (Button et al., 2013; De Boeck and Jeon, 2018; Open Science Collaboration, 2015), replicability of the previously reported SBB-associations were also questioned recently.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies documenting the replication crisis.

claim: Boekel et al. (2015) could not find support for almost all original SBB results in their replication attempt.
source: In particular, (Boekel et al., 2015) in a purely confirmatory replication study, picked on few specific previously reported SBB-associations. Strikingly, for almost all the findings under scrutiny, they could not find support for the original results in their replication attempt.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous replication study.

claim: Genon et al. (2017) demonstrated lack of robustness of the pattern of correlations between cognitive performance and measures of gray matter volume in a-priori defined sub-regions of the dorsal premotor cortex.
source: In another study we demonstrated lack of robustness of the pattern of correlations between cognitive performance and measures of gray matter volume (GMV) in a-priori defined sub-regions of the dorsal premotor cortex in two samples of healthy adults (Genon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Genon et al. (2017) found a considerable number of SBB-associations that were counterintuitive in their directions (i.e., higher performance related to lower gray matter volume).
source: In particular we found a considerable number of SBB-associations that were counterintuitive in their directions (i.e., higher performance related to lower gray matter volume).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Subsampling revealed that for a given psychological score, negative correlations with GMV were as likely as positive correlations.
source: Furthermore, subsampling revealed that for a given psychological score, negative correlations with GMV were as likely as positive correlations.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Boekel et al. and Genon et al.'s studies were performed by focusing on a-priori defined regions-of-interest (ROIs).
source: In particular, Boekel et al. and Genon et al.'s studies were performed by focusing on a-priori defined regions-of-interest (ROIs).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in previous studies.

claim: Several SBB studies are commonly performed in groups of dozens of individuals, using an exploratory setting employing a mass-univariate approach.
source: However, several SBB studies are commonly performed in groups of dozens of individuals, using an exploratory setting employing a mass-univariate approach.
evidence: This is stated as a description of common practice in the field.

claim: In whole-brain mass-univariate exploratory SBB studies, the multitude of statistical tests likely yield many false positives.
source: In stark contrast with this argument, in whole-brain mass-univariate exploratory SBB studies, the multitude of statistical tests that is performed (as the associations are tested for each voxel, separately) likely yield many false positives.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical principles about multiple testing.

claim: Several strategies for multiple comparison correction have been proposed to control the rate of false positives.
source: Directly addressing this limitation, several strategies for multiple comparison correction have been proposed to control the rate of false positives (Eklund et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The high number of multiple tests and general low power of neuroimaging studies, combined with flexible analysis choices, represent critical factors likely to lead to the detection of spurious and not replicable associations.
source: We could hence assume that the high number of multiple tests and general low power of neuroimaging studies, combined with the flexible analysis choices (Button et al., 2013; Poldrack et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2018) represent critical factors likely to lead to the detection of spurious and not replicable associations.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yuan and Raz (2014) focused on SBB within the frontal lobe based on a sample made of approximately 80% of ROI studies.
source: For example, (Yuan and Raz, 2014) have focused on SBB within the frontal lobe based on a sample made of approximately 80% of ROI studies.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous meta-analysis.

claim: The mass-univariate approach is still the main workhorse tool in SBB studies.
source: The mass-univariate approach is still the main workhorse tool in such studies, not only due to its historical precedence and its wide integration in common neuroimaging tools, but also possibly owing to more straightforward interpretability of the detected effects (Smith and Nichols, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a description of current practice in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The mass-univariate approach is preferred partly due to more straightforward interpretability of the detected effects.
source: The mass-univariate approach is still the main workhorse tool in such studies, not only due to its historical precedence and its wide integration in common neuroimaging tools, but also possibly owing to more straightforward interpretability of the detected effects (Smith and Nichols, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a reason for the preference of the mass-univariate approach, supported by a citation.

claim: A total of 10800 exploratory whole brain SBB associations were tested in the study.
source: A total of 10800 exploratory whole brain SBB associations (each with 1000 permutations) were tested to empirically identify the replicability of the associations of 36 psychological scores with GMV over 100 splits in independent matched subsamples, at three pre-defined sample sizes, within the healthy cohort
evidence: This is a description of the study design and data.

claim: For the majority of the tested psychological variables no significant association with GMV were found in more than 90% of the whole brain analyses.
source: For the majority of the tested psychological variables no significant association with GMV were found in more than 90% of the whole brain analyses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's empirical investigation.

claim: Voxel-wise associations of age and BMI with GMV were widespread and strong.
source: Voxel-wise associations of age and BMI with GMV, as suggested by previous studies (Fjell et al., 2014; Kharabian Masouleh et al., 2016; Salat et al., 2004; Willette and Kapogiannis, 2015), were widespread and strong.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: For almost all subsamples, highly consistent widespread negative associations of GMV with age were found.
source: Despite using more stringent thresholds, compared to the threshold used for the psychological scores (see Materials and methods), for almost all subsamples, we found highly consistent widespread negative associations of GMV with age.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: When decreasing the sample size of the discovery cohort, the spatial overlap of significant findings over 100 splits decreased for age associations.
source: When decreasing the sample size of the discovery cohort, the spatial overlap of significant findings over 100 splits decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1.

claim: For the discovery sample of 326 subjects, more than half of the significant voxels were consistently found as being significant in beyond 90% of the whole-brain exploratory analyses for age.
source: More specifically, for the discovery sample of 326 subjects, more than half of the significant voxels were consistently found as being significant in beyond 90% of the whole-brain exploratory analyses (i.e. high level of spatial consistency of significant findings).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1.

claim: For BMI, few voxels were consistently found in 'all' (100%) subsamples as having significant negative association for larger samples (consisting of 326 and 232 subjects).
source: The density plots and the spatial maps of Figure 1B show that for the larger samples (consisting of 326 and 232 subjects) few voxels were consistently found in 'all' (100%) subsamples as having significant negative association with BMI.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For smaller samples with 138 participants, the maximum replicable association for BMI was found in 93% of the splits.
source: For the smaller samples (with 138 participants) the maximum replicable association was found in 93% of the splits and 4 out of 100 exploratory analyses did not result in any significant clusters (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Table 1.

claim: 4 out of 100 exploratory analyses did not result in any significant clusters for BMI in smaller samples with 138 participants.
source: For the smaller samples (with 138 participants) the maximum replicable association was found in 93% of the splits and 4 out of 100 exploratory analyses did not result in any significant clusters (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Table 1.

claim: For most of the psychological scores, only few of the 100 discovery subsamples yielded significant clusters.
source: In contrast, for most of the psychological scores, only few of the 100 discovery subsamples yielded significant clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Finding significant SBB-associations using the exploratory approach in healthy individuals is highly unlikely for most of the psychological variables.
source: These results reveal that finding significant SBB-associations using the exploratory approach in healthy individuals is highly unlikely for most of the psychological variables.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The significant findings for psychological scores were spatially very diverse, that is, spatially overlapping findings were very rare.
source: Furthermore, the significant findings were spatially very diverse, that is, spatially overlapping findings were very rare.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The three psychological scores for which the discovery samples most frequently resulted in at least one significantly associated cluster were the Perceptual reasoning score of WASI, the number of correct responses in word-context test and the interference time in the color-word interference task.
source: We here retained for further analyses the three psychological scores for which the discovery samples most frequently resulted in at least one significantly associated cluster. These three scores were the Perceptual reasoning score of WASI (Wechsler, 1999), the number of correct responses in word-context test and the interference time in the color-word interference task.
evidence: This is a description of the study's selection criteria and findings.

claim: For the discovery samples of 326 adults, in 83 out of 100 randomly generated discovery samples, at least one cluster showed a significant positive association between perceptual reasoning and GMV.
source: For example, for the discovery samples of 326 adults, in 83 out of 100 randomly generated discovery samples, at least one cluster (not necessarily overlapping) showed a significant positive association between perceptual reasoning and GMV (Table 1)).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Table 1.

claim: The more frequently found associations were in the direction linking better task performance with higher GMV.
source: Of note, these more frequently found associations were in the direction linking better task performance with higher GMV.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The probability of finding at least one significant cluster tends to decrease in smaller discovery samples for psychological scores.
source: Yet again, in line with our observations for BMI associations, the probability of finding at least one significant cluster tend to decrease in smaller discovery samples (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Table 1.

claim: As the discovery sample size decreased, the maximum rate of spatial overlap decreased for psychological scores.
source: Likewise, as the discovery sample size decreased, the maximum rate of spatial overlap, as denoted by the height of the density plots, decreased (see Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1.

claim: The majority (>50%) of the significant voxels for psychological scores spatially overlapped only in less than 10% of the discovery samples.
source: The width of these plots show that the majority (>50%) of the significant voxels spatially overlapped only in less than 10% of the discovery samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 1.

claim: Irrespective of the size of the test subsamples and definition used to identify 'successful' replication, for all ROIs negative age-GMV associations were 'successfully' replicated in the matched test samples.
source: Irrespective of the size of the test subsamples and definition used to identify 'successful' replication (see Materials and methods), for all ROIs negative age-GMV associations were 'successfully' replicated in the matched test samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Over all three tested sample sizes, in more than 90% of the a-priori defined ROIs, BMI associations were found to be in the same 'direction' in the discovery and test samples.
source: Over all three tested sample sizes, in more than 90% of the a-priori defined ROIs, BMI associations were found to be in the same 'direction' in the discovery and test samples (i.e. replicated based on 'sign' criteria).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: The examination of replicated findings based on 'statistical significance' revealed replicated effects in more than 57% of ROIs for BMI.
source: The examination of replicated findings based on 'statistical significance' revealed replicated effects in more than 57% of ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rate of ROI-based replicability for BMI increased from ~57% to 75%, as the test sample size increased from 140 to 328 individuals.
source: This rate of ROI-based replicability increased from ~57% to 75%, as the test sample size increased from 140 to 328 individuals (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Bayesian hypothesis testing revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for H1 in more than 30% of the ROIs for BMI.
source: Furthermore, as the dark blue segments in the outer layers of Figure 2 indicates, Bayesian hypothesis testing revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for H1 in more than 30% of the ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Despite the structural associations of perceptual reasoning score being in the same direction (positive SBB-association) for the majority of the ROIs (>85%), less than 31% of all ROIs showed replicated effects based on 'statistical significance' criterion.
source: Despite the structural associations of perceptual reasoning score being in the same direction (positive SBB-association), for the majority of the ROIs (>85%), less than 31% of all ROIs showed replicated effects based on 'statistical significance' criterion.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Less than 4% of the ROIs for perceptual reasoning were identified as 'successfully replicated' based on the Bayes factors.
source: Finally, less than 4% of the ROIs were identified as 'successfully replicated' based on the Bayes factors. (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: For the three tested samples sizes, associations of the word-context task were in the same direction (positive SBB-association) in the discovery and test pairs in ~75% of ROIs.
source: For the three tested samples sizes, associations of the word-context task were in the same direction (positive SBB-association) in the discovery and test pairs in ~75% of ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rate of statistically 'significantly'-replicated ROIs for word-context task ranged between 17% to 26%.
source: Nevertheless, again, the rate of statistically 'significantly'-replicated ROIs ranged between 17% to 26%.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Less than 8% of all ROIs for word-context task showed replicated effects based on the Bayes factors (moderate-to-strong evidence for H1).
source: Furthermore, even less than 8% of all ROIs showed replicated effects based on the Bayes factors (moderate-to-strong evidence for H1) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Negative correlations between interference time of the color-word interference task and average GMV were depicted in ~70% of the ROIs.
source: Finally, negative correlations between interference time of the color-word interference task and average GMV were depicted in ~70% of the ROIs, but significant-replication was found in only 11% to 17% of all ROIs, for the three test sample sizes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significant-replication for color-word interference task was found in only 11% to 17% of all ROIs, for the three test sample sizes.
source: Finally, negative correlations between interference time of the color-word interference task and average GMV were depicted in ~70% of the ROIs, but significant-replication was found in only 11% to 17% of all ROIs, for the three test sample sizes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Replication based on the Bayes factors for color-word interference task was below 5%.
source: Along the same line, replication based on the Bayes factors was below 5% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: For the three psychological scores (perceptual reasoning, word-context and CWI), the discovery samples resulted in overall larger effects (magnitude) compared to the test samples.
source: Focusing on by-'sign' replicated ROIs (blue), for the three psychological scores (perceptual reasoning, word-context and CWI) revealed that the discovery samples resulted in overall larger effects (magnitude) compared to the test samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3.

claim: For by-'sign' replicated ROIs of the three psychological scores, there was no positive relationship between the effect sizes of the behavioral associations in the discovery and test samples.
source: Furthermore, for these by-'sign' replicated ROIs, there was no positive relationship between the effect sizes of the behavioral associations in the discovery and test samples (blue lines in each subplot).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3.

claim: For BMI and age, the effect sizes of the discovery and test pairs were generally positively correlated.
source: For BMI and age, however, the effect sizes of the discovery and test pairs were generally positively correlated, suggesting that the ROIs with greater negative structural association with BMI (or age) in the discovery sample, also tended to show stronger negative associations within the matched test sample.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3.

claim: ROIs with greater negative structural association with BMI (or age) in the discovery sample tended to show stronger negative associations within the matched test sample.
source: For BMI and age, however, the effect sizes of the discovery and test pairs were generally positively correlated, suggesting that the ROIs with greater negative structural association with BMI (or age) in the discovery sample, also tended to show stronger negative associations within the matched test sample.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the positive correlation between discovery and test effect sizes.

claim: The estimations of statistical power were generally higher among the replicated compared to not-replicated ROIs for BMI associations (p-value of the Mann-Whitney U tests <10−5).
source: While the estimations of statistical power were generally higher among the replicated compared to not-replicated ROIs for BMI associations (p-value of the Mann-Whitney U tests <10−5), for structural associations of the psychological scores, this was not the case.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: For the structural associations of perceptual reasoning, over all sample sizes, the significantly replicated ROIs tended to have lower estimated power compared to the ROIs that actually were not-replicated (p-value of the Mann-Whitney U tests <10−5).
source: Strikingly, for the structural associations of perceptual reasoning, over all sample sizes, the significantly replicated ROIs tended to have lower estimated power compared to the ROIs that actually were not-replicated (p-value of the Mann-Whitney U tests <10−5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Within the sample of patients from ADNI-cohort, 84 out of the 100 whole-brain exploratory analyses resulted in at least one significant cluster showing a positive association between the immediate-recall score and GMV.
source: Within the sample of patients from ADNI-cohort, 84 out of the 100 whole-brain exploratory analyses resulted in at least one significant cluster showing a positive association between the immediate-recall score and GMV.
evidence: This is a finding from the study in the ADNI cohort.

claim: In the healthy population, the immediate-recall score resulted in a significant cluster in only less than 10% of exploratory analyses, for any of the three discovery sample sizes.
source: In the healthy population, however, the same score resulted in a significant cluster in only less than 10% of exploratory analyses, for any of the three discovery sample sizes (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing healthy and clinical populations.

claim: Significant associations in the ADNI cohort were found across several brain regions including the bilateral lateral and medial temporal lobe, the lateral occipital cortex, the precuneus, the superior parietal lobule, the orbitofrontal cortex and the thalamus.
source: As could be seen in the spatial maps of Figure 4, significant associations in the ADNI cohort were found across several brain regions including the bilateral lateral and medial temporal lobe, the lateral occipital cortex, the precuneus, the superior parietal lobule, the orbitofrontal cortex and the thalamus.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4.

claim: Some voxels in the bilateral hippocampus were found to be significantly associated with the recall score in more than 70% of the subsamples in the ADNI cohort.
source: Although most of the significant voxels were found by less than 10% of the splits, some voxels in the bilateral hippocampus were found to be significantly associated with the recall score in more than 70% of the subsamples (peak of spatial overlap; see Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4.

claim: In more than 94% of ROIs in the ADNI cohort, GMV correlated positively with the recall score in the test subsamples, corroborating the 'sign' of the association in the paired-discovery samples.
source: As the most inner layer shows, in more than 94% of ROIs, GMV correlated positively with the recall score in the test subsamples, corroborating the 'sign' of the association in the paired-discovery samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the ADNI cohort, the correlations between GMV and recall score were significant in 72% of all ROIs.
source: These correlations were significant in 72% of all ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In more than 50% of all ROIs in the ADNI cohort, the correlations in the test sample supported, at least moderately, the link between higher GMV and higher recall score (using the Bayes factors).
source: Furthermore, in more than 50% of all ROIs the correlations in the test sample supported, at least moderately, the link between higher GMV and higher recall score (using the Bayes factors).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overall the correlations in the discovery samples are slightly stronger than the correlations in the paired replication samples in the ADNI cohort.
source: The marginal histograms in Figure 4C suggest that overall the correlations in the discovery samples are slightly stronger than the correlations in the paired replication samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When looking at the ROIs that were successfully replicated (by-sign) in the ADNI cohort, there was a positive association between the discovery and replication effect size (spearman's rho = 0.38, p-value<10−11).
source: When looking at the ROIs that were successfully replicated (by-sign), there was a positive association between the discovery and replication effect size (spearman's rho = 0.38, p-value<10−11).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The median replication power was higher among 'significantly replicated' ROIs, compared to not replicated ROIs in the ADNI cohort (p-value of the mann-whiteney U test <10−3).
source: Finally, the median replication power was higher among 'significantly replicated' ROIs, compared to not replicated (defined using 'statistical significance criterion') ROIs (p-value of the mann-whiteney U test <10−3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: When the population under study shows clear variations in both brain structural markers and psychological measurements, such as the patient group in ADNI cohort, the associations between brain structure and psychological performance could be relatively reliably characterized.
source: These results showed the superior, yet not perfect, replicability of SBB-associations within the clinical population (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for structural associations of immediate recall within healthy cohort). The observed somewhat robustness of the findings in ADNI suggest that, when the population under study shows clear variations in both brain structural markers and psychological measurements, such as the patient group in ADNI cohort, the associations between brain structure and psychological performance could be relatively reliably characterized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of findings in healthy and clinical populations.

claim: The occurrence of not-replicated results in the ADNI cohort highlights the importance of confirmatory analyses for a robust characterization of brain-behavior associations.
source: Nevertheless, again, the occurrence of not-replicated results highlight the importance of confirmatory analyses for a robust characterization of brain-behavior associations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings.

claim: Significant associations between psychological phenotype and GMV are not frequent when probing a range of psychometric variables with an exploratory approach in healthy adults.
source: Our empirical investigation of the replicability of SBB in healthy adults showed that significant associations between psychological phenotype and GMV are not frequent when probing a range of psychometric variables with an exploratory approach.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Where significant associations were found in healthy adults, these associations showed a poor replicability.
source: Our empirical investigation of the replicability of SBB in healthy adults showed that significant associations between psychological phenotype and GMV are not frequent when probing a range of psychometric variables with an exploratory approach. Where significant associations were found, these associations showed a poor replicability.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Flexible designs and flexible analyses routines as well as p-hacking are considered as inappropriate but frequent research practices.
source: Flexible designs and flexible analyses routines (Simmons et al., 2011) as well as p-hacking (John et al., 2012) are considered as inappropriate but frequent research practices (Poldrack et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Flexible analyses routines, p-hacking and publication bias have contributed to the high number of significant SBB-reports in the literature.
source: Based on our findings of infrequent significant SBB-associations, we could assume that flexible analyses routines, p-hacking and most importantly publication bias (Dwan et al., 2013) have contributed to the high number of significant SBB-reports in the literature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Psychological measures aim to conceptually articulate behavioral functions and processes, thus, in most cases, they have not been developed to identify specific localized brain functions.
source: Psychological measures aim to conceptually articulate behavioral functions and processes, thus, in most cases, they have not been developed to identify specific localized brain functions.
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual argument about the nature of psychological measures.

claim: There is no one-to-one mapping between behavioral functions and brain regions.
source: Following this philosophical segregation between psychological sciences and neurosciences, it is now widely acknowledged that there is no one-to-one mapping between behavioral functions and brain regions (Anderson, 2016; Genon et al., 2018; Pessoa, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mapping a psychological concept to brain features usually result in a diffuse brain spatial pattern with small effect sizes.
source: Instead, mapping a psychological concept to brain features usually result in a diffuse brain spatial pattern with small effect sizes (Bressler, 1995; Poldrack, 2010; Tononi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several studies conducted in small samples are likely to each capture a partial and minor aspect of the whole true association pattern, resulting in a poor replication rate for each individual study.
source: From this axiom, we can expect that several studies conducted in small samples (specifically after rigorous corrections for multiple comparisons) are likely to each capture a partial and minor aspect of the whole true association pattern, resulting in a poor replication rate for each individual study (i.e. high type II error).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conceptual argument about diffuse brain patterns.

claim: Psychological and MRI measurements are both relatively indirect estimations of respectively, behavioral features and brain structural features and thus are susceptible to noise.
source: Psychological and MRI measurements are both relatively indirect estimations of respectively, behavioral features and brain structural features and thus are susceptible to noise.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: Correlations in small samples in the presence of noise for both type of variables is likely to produce spurious significant results.
source: Correlations in small samples in the presence of noise for both type of variables is likely to produce spurious significant results (Loken and Gelman, 2017) by fitting a correlation or regression between random noise in both variables.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration supported by a citation.

claim: The pattern of poor spatial consistency of SBB findings could result either from factors at the object of study level, that is the relationship between brain and behavior, or, from factors at the measurement and analysis level.
source: Thus, the pattern of poor spatial consistency of SBB findings could result either from factors at the object of study level, that is the relationship between brain and behavior, or, from factors at the measurement and analysis level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible causes.

claim: It is likely that both hypotheses hold true and that the spatial variability of significant SBB findings result from both, factors at the analyses levels and factors at the object level, potentially interacting together.
source: Therefore, it is actually likely that both hypotheses hold true and that the spatial variability of significant SBB findings result from both, factors at the analyses levels and factors at the object level, potentially interacting together.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the causes of the findings.

claim: Cremers et al. (2017) using simulated and empirical data demonstrated that task-based functional activations have a generally weak and diffuse pattern.
source: In particular, Cremers et al. (2017) using simulated and empirical data demonstrated that task-based functional activations have a generally weak and diffuse pattern.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: Most whole-brain analyses in small samples, specifically when combined with stringent correction for multiple comparison, would most likely frequently overlook global meaningful effects and depict results with poor replicability.
source: Therefore, these authors concluded that most whole-brain analyses in small samples, specifically when combined with stringent correction for multiple comparison, to control the false positive rates, would most likely frequently overlook global meaningful effects and depict results with poor replicability (type II error).
evidence: This is a citation to conclusions from a previous study.

claim: Higher spatial extent and lower consistency of significant findings in smaller samples suggest higher number of spurious associations (type I error) in smaller samples.
source: Relatedly, in the present study, higher spatial extent and lower consistency of significant findings in smaller samples in Figure 1, also suggest higher number of spurious associations (type I error) in smaller samples (due to winners curse [Button et al., 2013; Forstmeier and Schielzeth, 2011]) than in larger samples.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: In exploratory studies whose aim is to identify brain structural features correlating with a specific (set of) psychological variable(s), a multivariate approach could be advised.
source: For that reason, in exploratory studies whose aim is to identify brain structural features correlating with a specific (set of) psychological variable(s), a multivariate approach could be advised (Habeck et al., 2010; McIntosh and Mišić, 2013).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: Combining univariate and multivariate approaches in small datasets revealed that the results of the univariate approach reflect the 'tip of the iceberg' of the behavior's brain correlates.
source: Combining both approaches in small datasets indeed revealed that the results of the univariate approach reflect the 'tip of the iceberg' of the behavior's brain correlates, whose spatial extent are more comprehensively captured with the multivariate analysis, but interpretability is facilitated by the use of univariate analyses; for example (Genon et al., 2016; Genon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The spatial extent of behavior's brain correlates are more comprehensively captured with the multivariate analysis, but interpretability is facilitated by the use of univariate analyses.
source: Combining both approaches in small datasets indeed revealed that the results of the univariate approach reflect the 'tip of the iceberg' of the behavior's brain correlates, whose spatial extent are more comprehensively captured with the multivariate analysis, but interpretability is facilitated by the use of univariate analyses; for example (Genon et al., 2016; Genon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Significant associations, which have been discovered when starting with a psychological measure and searching within the whole brain for a significant association, show poor replicability in a confirmatory ROI-based study.
source: ROI-based analysis further highlighted that significant associations, which have been discovered when starting with a psychological measure and searching within the whole brain for a significant association (i.e. 'evidenced in an exploratory study'), show poor replicability (using significance and Bayes factor criteria, but also using a similar sign criterion for most psychometric scores; For example, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) in a confirmatory ROI-based study (in line with what was previously shown by Boekel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by citations and references to figures.

claim: There is a need for out of sample confirmatory replications to provide evidence about the robustness of the reported effects.
source: These findings thus call for a general acknowledgment of the uncertainty and fragility of exploratory findings and the need for out of sample confirmatory replications to provide evidence about the robustness of the reported effects (Ioannidis, 2018; Tukey, 1980).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: There is overestimation of the effect size in the exploratory approach, specifically in smaller samples.
source: Another clear finding of our study is the overestimation of the effect size in the exploratory approach (Kriegeskorte et al., 2010), specifically in smaller samples (see marginal distributions of the x- and y-axis in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 3.

claim: For the majority of the psychological scores, in the ROI-based approach, the study failed to find a clear association between effect size in the discovery and replication samples.
source: For the majority of the psychological scores, in the ROI-based approach, we failed to find a clear association between effect size in the discovery and replication samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: A rather high estimated statistical power for replication was observed (due to an inflated effect size estimation), despite very low actual rate of replicated effects in the independent samples.
source: Instead, we observed a rather high estimated statistical power for replication (due to an inflated effect size estimation [Ioannidis, 2008]), despite very low actual rate of replicated effects in the independent samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by a citation.

claim: An inflated effect size estimation from the exploratory study results in an unreliable high power, which in turn lead to confidence in prospective studies to find relevant findings and hence in the allocation and possibly waste of resources.
source: An inflated effect size estimation from the exploratory study results in an unreliable high power, which in turn lead to confidence in prospective studies to find relevant findings and hence in the allocation and possibly waste of (frequently public) resources (Albers and Lakens, 2018; Poldrack et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: In ADNI sample, despite the additional confounding effect of different scanners and/or scanning parameters due to the multi-site nature of the cohort, associations between immediate-recall score and GMV were relatively stable.
source: In support for this argument, in ADNI sample, despite the additional confounding effect of different scanners and/or scanning parameters due to the multi-site nature of the cohort, associations between immediate-recall score and GMV were relatively stable.
evidence: This is a finding from the study in the ADNI cohort.

claim: The comparative investigation suggests that the object of study matters in the replicability of SBB.
source: From an epistemological and conceptual point of view, our comparative investigation suggests that the object of study matters in the replicability of SBB.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of findings in healthy and clinical populations.

claim: Searching for correlation between variations in cognitive performance and GMV in healthy adults, on one hand, and in neurodegenerative patients, on the other hand, appear as two different objects of study, with different replicability rates.
source: Searching for correlation between variations in cognitive performance and GMV in healthy adults, on one hand, and in neurodegenerative patients, on the other hand, appear as two different objects of study, with different replicability rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of findings in healthy and clinical populations.

claim: Several SBB results in healthy population are likely to be spurious.
source: While several SBB results in healthy population are likely to be spurious (see Supplementary file 2), it seems that SBB in clinical population are more likely to capture true relationships.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: SBB in clinical population are more likely to capture true relationships.
source: While several SBB results in healthy population are likely to be spurious (see Supplementary file 2), it seems that SBB in clinical population are more likely to capture true relationships.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Reliable answer to whether 'normal' variations at standard psychological tests can be related to variations in markers of local brain macrostructure requires substantially big samples and independent replications.
source: Our results suggest that reliable answer to this important question requires substantially big samples (bigger than those used here) and independent replications.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: High power experiments have higher positive predictive values (PPV) of the claimed effects.
source: Furthermore, high power experiments have higher positive predictive values (PPV) of the claimed effects (i.e. probability that the claimed effect reflects a true effect).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about statistical power.

claim: High power experiments result in less exaggerated effects sizes when a true effect is discovered.
source: They also result in less exaggerated effects sizes when a true effect is discovered (Button et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about statistical power, supported by a citation.

claim: Samples consisting of ~200–300 participants have in reality still low power to identify reliable SBB-associations among healthy participants.
source: Thus overall, these findings suggest that samples consisting of ~200–300 participants have in reality still low power to identify reliable SBB-associations among healthy participants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The probability of finding spurious or inconclusive results and exaggerated effect size estimations in SBB studies with small sample sizes is quite high.
source: Based on our current work, we would argue that the probability of finding spurious or inconclusive results and exaggerated effect size estimations in these studies is thus quite high (Albers and Lakens, 2018; Schönbrodt and Perugini, 2013; Yarkoni, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: The size of the replication sample matters when examining the replicability of a previous SBB findings.
source: In addition, to underscore the importance of the sample size, our analyses and results further show that the size of the replication sample also matters when examining the replicability of a previous SBB findings.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: A replication failure might also come from a too small sample size of the replication study.
source: Yet, while many replication studies straightforwardly blame the sample size of the original studies, it is important to keep in mind that a replication failure might also come from a too small sample size of the replication study (Muhlert and Ridgway, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a consideration about replication studies, supported by a citation.

claim: The discovery subsamples were not necessarily designed to be independent from each other.
source: When interpreting our results, it should be noted that, in order to keep large sample sizes for the exploratory replication analyses, the discovery subsamples were not necessarily designed to be independent from each other.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the study.

claim: The limited size of the selected cohort results in dependence between the size of the discovery and their matched replication sub-samples.
source: As discussed earlier, another indirect limitation of the limited size of the selected cohort is the dependence between the size of the discovery and their matched replication sub-samples.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the study.

claim: Large scale cohort datasets from healthy adult populations, such as eNKI, HCP and UK-biobank are now openly available.
source: Nevertheless, large scale cohort datasets from healthy adult populations, such as eNKI used in the current study, human connectome project (HCP) (WU-Minn HCP Consortium et al., 2013) and UK-biobank (Miller et al., 2016) are now openly available, hence facilitating endeavor in that direction.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about available datasets, supported by citations.

claim: Publication of null findings should be more encouraged.
source: Finally, at the post-analysis level, we concluded from our observations that publication of null findings should be more encouraged.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Sharing raw data would undoubtedly improve the problem of low statistical power.
source: Sharing raw data would undoubtedly improve the problem of low statistical power, but if not possible, sharing the unthresholded statistical maps (e.g. through platforms such as Neurovault [Gorgolewski et al., 2015]) could also be a significant scientific contribution.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Sharing the unthresholded statistical maps could be a significant scientific contribution.
source: Sharing raw data would undoubtedly improve the problem of low statistical power, but if not possible, sharing the unthresholded statistical maps (e.g. through platforms such as Neurovault [Gorgolewski et al., 2015]) could also be a significant scientific contribution.
